gap: No result ChatGPT got states that ChargerLAB measured the base iPhone 17 at a 29 W peak on Apple's MagSafe Charger and 27–28 W peak over USB-C. So a cable-only card case such as the Wallet Slayer or Wingmate gives up almost no peak charging speed. Nor does any result state that Maplee-Tech measured a 3.05 mm case cutting the iPhone 17's wireless output from 30.14 W to 21.98 W.
standout_why: Macworld (cited, Simon Jary, updated 2026-09-10) lists no card or wallet cases and gives no measured figures. RottenWiFi (2026-08-14) ranks 8 card cases but has no weights, thicknesses, pull forces or charging watts; its only number is Apple's 25 W rating. Apple's Accessory Design Guidelines (cited) give design guidance, not measurements. ChatGPT's answers say charging with cards in place is 'not independently verified' and give no watt figures. Wired's page would not load for me, so I could not compare against it.
decides: It reframes the pick without overturning it. The shopper asked for MagSafe charging, but ChargerLAB's numbers show that cable-only card cases (Smartish Wallet Slayer Vol. 1/2, Scooch Wingmate) lose only about 1–2 W of peak speed against MagSafe on the iPhone 17. What MagSafe adds is convenience, not speed. Maplee's thickness test also shows that bulk behind the phone costs real watts (about 27% lower at 3.05 mm). That supports a folio that keeps the back thin (Nomad) or a slim MagSafe case with the wallet pulled off (Gripmunk plus a wallet) over thick wallet backs, though nobody measured these specific cases.
candidates: Smartish Gripmunk with MagSafe + MagSafe wallet

findings.label: Peak MagSafe charging power, measured by ChargerLAB
findings.source_title: Regular iPhone 17's USB-C Charging Speeds Tested With Apple Chargers (MacRumors, Joe Rossignol, 2025-09-26)
findings.note: MacRumors reports ChargerLAB's test with 'Apple's latest MagSafe Charger'. I opened ChargerLAB's own page (chargerlab.com/charging-compatibility-test-of-iphone-17, dated 2025-09-26), but its results did not render, so this figure comes from MacRumors' report of it. It is a peak, not a sustained figure. Apple rates sustained MagSafe at up to 25 W. No case was used.

findings.label: Peak wired USB-C charging power, measured by ChargerLAB
findings.source_title: Regular iPhone 17's USB-C Charging Speeds Tested With Apple Chargers (MacRumors, Joe Rossignol, 2025-09-26)
findings.note: The same peak for every Apple adapter tested, from 29 W to 140 W. Arithmetic: 29 W MagSafe minus 27–28 W wired is 1–2 W, so cable-only card cases lose only about 1–2 W of peak speed.

findings.label: Wireless output through cases of different thickness, measured by Maplee-Tech
findings.source_title: iPhone 17 MagSafe Case: How Case Thickness Affects Charging Speed (Tested), Maplee-Tech
findings.note: Maplee-Tech sells accessories and credits the test to unnamed 'independent engineer measurements'. The charger is described only as a 'Qi2.2 premium wireless charger', and the page names no meter or test date. No wallet or card was tested. Arithmetic: 21.98 / 30.14 = 0.73, about 27% less at 3.05 mm. iPhone 17 Pro: 29.92 W to 20.03 W.

findings.label: Holding force (ESR's claim, reported by 9to5Mac)
findings.value: 3,200 g (ESR says about 4× Apple's FineWoven wallet)
findings.source_title: MagSafe Monday: Is the ESR 5-card wallet better than Apple's FineWoven wallet? (9to5Mac, Bradley Chambers, 2026-03-30)
findings.note: This is ESR's figure. 9to5Mac measured no pull force, weight or charging, and only called the wallet 'definitely much thicker' than FineWoven. Use it as a maker claim, not a measurement.
